b01: Most people building community do the steps in the wrong order. Sound familiar? They get the land first, put the vision in a document, let ownership pile up with whoever had the money, and put off the emotional preparation until everyone has more time.
b02:
Most people building community do the steps in the wrong order. Sound familiar? They get the land first, put the vision in a document, let ownership pile up with whoever had the money, and put off the emotional preparation until everyone has more time.

The better order is less cinematic, more like this: practice together, process a real conflict, clarify your values, test membership, decide ownership and exit, and only then think about land. I know, it wouldn't make much of a movie!
b03:
People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed baggage with them to a more scenic location. The view's better, I'll give them that! But now the conflict has goats.

But there's no reason you can't start the inner pl/ork where you live. And peer counseling? It only needs two people and enough privacy to talk. Reparenting, somatic work, jealousy, conflict repair and the rest don't have to wait for a deed either!
b04:
Remote or constrained readers can build the portion available. Hold a weekly meal with two households. Arrange a counseling exchange with one friend in person or by video. Share tools and childcare, or transport and food preparation. Or a sauna! Add acro-yoga, dance improvisation, a mothers' circle, or a cuddle puddle if you're hippie enough.

Trust me on this one. If three households can commit to showing up for each other like this for six months, you'll learn more than you would from another year of daydreaming about the ideal village.
b05:
Where do you find them? Maybe try unprogrammed Quaker meetings, restorative practice groups, open-hearted congregations, mature recovery groups, meditation groups, or people who came back from a long retreat kinder rather than more impressed with themselves.

Then go visit actual communities, like Twin Oaks, East Wind, Acorn or other intentional communities (a lot of ecovillages take visitors too). Ever been to one? Just check their current visitor requirements first.

What do you get out of a visit? Stuff no manifesto can tell you: how much togetherness you actually enjoy, what kind of privacy you need, which labor system drives you nuts, and whether communal showers feel liberating or send you off pricing studio apartments.
